misconceptions.description: Listing a tool name as the transferable skill instead of the underlying capability it represents
misconceptions.trigger: transfer map row says 'Excel' or 'GitHub' in the skill column with no described capability
misconceptions.feedback: Map the capability, not the brand. 'Built a pivot table to summarize 500 rows' transfers to Google Sheets and a job dashboard; 'Excel' alone does not.

misconceptions.description: Claiming a skill transfers to a new context without naming the specific task it would do there
misconceptions.trigger: row says 'HTML transfers to my future career' with no concrete task
misconceptions.feedback: Name the destination task. 'I can edit the company GitHub Pages site by changing the <h2> headings in index.html' is a verifiable transfer claim.

misconceptions.description: Assuming a CAT 100 procedure works unchanged in a new context that has a different constraint
misconceptions.trigger: learner copies a course workflow into a job setting without checking the new constraint
misconceptions.feedback: Transfer adapts, it does not copy. A formula that worked on 40 class rows may need an absolute reference ($A$1) or a different range when the job dataset has 4,000 rows.

misconceptions.description: Accepting an AI tool's suggested formula or fix without judging it against the destination context, and not documenting the modified or rejected part of the suggestion
misconceptions.trigger: adaptation note says 'used Copilot' or 'used AI' with no recorded accept/modify/reject decision
misconceptions.feedback: Judge AI output against the new context, then document the boundary. Copilot in Excel can offer a relative-range fill that drifts over 4,000 rows; the defensible move is modify (anchor the range) and record what you rejected and why.
